newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba retracts permission for new Spanish ambassador.
newsitem.headline: Cuba retracts permission for new Spanish ambassador.

text.p: Cuba has retracted its approval for a new Spanish ambassador to the country, diplomatic sources said on Tuesday.
The decision brought to a head a simmering dispute between Cuba and Spain over calls by the government of Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar for political change on the communist-ruled island.

The diplomatic sources said that the Cuban Foreign Ministry was announcing its decision in a statement published in Tuesday's edition of Communist Party newspaper Granma. The newspaper was not yet available on the street.

The sources quoted the statement as saying it was revoking the so-called "placet" (approval) for new ambassador Jose Coderch. Coderch had been named by Aznar's government, which took power in May, to replace current ambassador Eudaldo Mirapeix.
Coderch's placet was approved last month and he had been due to arrive in early December in Havana to take up his post.

The Foreign Ministry statement, quoted by the diplomatic sources, strongly criticised comments made in recent weeks by Aznar, Foreign Minister Abel Matutes and Coderch himself, and particularly singled out a plan by Spain to seek to persuade the European Union to adopt a single policy on Cuba following Madrid's line.
The statement said that the Spanish officials' declarations had offended the government and people of Cuba and constituted an unacceptable interference in Cuban affairs, the sources said.

The statement listed a series of declarations by the Aznar government, including an interview given by Coderch to the Spanish newspaper ABC last month, and a meeting at a Latin American summit in Chile earlier this month between Aznar and President Fidel Castro.
On these occasions the Spanish conservative government has made plain it intends a tougher line on Cuba than its socialist predecessor, saying it is seeking democratic change.

Cuba also objected strongly to a move by Spain two weeks ago to press the European Union to adopt a single policy on Cuba that followed its own. The statement, quoted by diplomatic sources, accused Spain of creating an interfering plan that sought to condition cooperation with Cuba and mirrored the aims of the United States -- which has long sought to press Havana into change.
The statement called the plan an extremely unfriendly act that the people and government of Cuba could not understand.

It also objected to the recent formation in Spain of a Cuban exile opposition group that includes members of Aznar's ruling Partido Popular (Popular Party) and Miami-based exile leader Jorge Mas Canosa, and aims to seek change in Cuba.

Tuesday's move was preceeded by strong statements against the Aznar government by Castro himself. The Cuban leader poured scorn on the Aznar government in comments during a visit to Rome last month, and again criticised the Spanish leader in a speech in Havana at the weekend.
